payload.rationale: The Sep 17 PMMS reading of 6.95% followed a sharp 19 bp weekly jump from 6.76%, after a month of readings in the 6.65–6.76% range. YES requires the Sep 24 reading to be 7.02% or higher, i.e., a further rise of at least 7 bp on top of last week's spike. Unconditionally, weekly PMMS changes have a standard deviation of roughly 8–12 bp centered near zero, implying roughly a 20–25% chance of a +7 bp or larger move. Two adjustments push in opposite directions: (1) the PMMS is a weekly average, so if the underlying rate rose mid-to-late in the survey week and held, the following week's average mechanically starts higher, creating positive short-term autocorrelation after large jumps; (2) large weekly jumps are often partially retraced as bond markets stabilize. Weighing these, I estimate roughly 30%. Reason the estimate could be too high: if the Sep 17 spike was driven by a transient event (e.g., a Fed-meeting reaction) that has since partially reversed, rates could settle back toward 6.85–6.95%, well below the threshold. Reason it could be too low: if Treasury yields kept climbing after the survey window closed (momentum into the week of Sep 18–23), the full-week average could easily print above 7.02%, and the mechanical carry-through effect alone could deliver several basis points. Without any bond-yield or daily lender-rate data from Sep 17–19, I cannot tell which scenario is unfolding, so the estimate stays near the unconditional-plus-momentum baseline.
limitations: No Treasury yield, MBS spread, or daily lender-rate data after the Sep 17 publication; cannot observe intra-week direction.
Volatility assumptions for weekly PMMS changes are from general background knowledge, not a fitted model on current-regime data.
Unknown macro catalysts (Fed communications, inflation data) in the Sep 18–24 window could dominate.
Only five weekly observations supplied; no information on what caused the 19 bp jump.
